name: Accelerated orthodontics (AcceleDent / Propel)

lead: Accelerated orthodontics covers add-ons to braces or aligners aimed at reaching a straight smile sooner, from daily vibration devices (AcceleDent is one brand) and low-level light therapy to micro-perforations of the bone (Propel) and surgeries such as corticotomy and piezocision.

The aim is to boost bone remodelling around the tooth roots, gently or by injuring the outer bone to trigger a temporary burst of remodelling. According to a summary of a 2023 Cochrane review, evidence that non-surgical adjuncts shorten overall treatment is of low to very low certainty; surgical methods may speed movement more but have limited high-quality research.

paras: Vibration and light devices are used for a few minutes daily at home while in braces or aligners. Micro-perforation and surgical versions are done by an orthodontist or surgeon at points during treatment.
Surgical forms involve pain, swelling and procedural complications, and reviews note harms are not always reported transparently in trials. Non-surgical devices mainly add cost and daily routine.

chain: Vibration, light or surgery stimulates bone
angle.text: AcceleDent, light therapy and Propel micro-perforations are used with braces or aligners to shorten treatment and reach a straight smile sooner by stimulating bone remodelling. Reviews rate non-surgical versions as low-certainty evidence, while surgical versions have shown more effect.

lead: Accelerated orthodontics refers to adjuncts used with braces or clear aligners that aim to speed tooth movement and shorten treatment. For people straightening their teeth, the appeal is a finished smile sooner: aligned, evenly spaced teeth are among the most visible contributors to a polished lower face, and shorter treatment means less time in visible appliances. The adjuncts are commonly grouped as non-surgical methods, such as cyclic vibration devices (AcceleDent is one brand), low-level light therapy and micro-osteoperforations such as the Propel system, and surgical methods such as corticotomy, piezocision and periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics.[1]

Surgical procedures are intended to injure the outer bone layer and trigger a temporary burst of bone remodeling, called the regional acceleratory phenomenon.[1] Systematic reviews have examined these methods and their harms. According to a Grokipedia summary of a 2023 Cochrane review, evidence that non-surgical adjuncts meaningfully shorten overall treatment is of low to very low certainty.[1] Several randomized trials of the AcceleDent Aura vibration device have been published, most reporting no difference in tooth movement rate, while surgical approaches have been reported to speed movement more in some studies.[2][3][4]
infobox: Adjunctive treatments to braces or aligners
AcceleDent Aura described as a US FDA class II medical device[3]

paras: Orthodontic treatment moves teeth through bone by applying sustained light forces with braces, wires or clear aligners. Adult patients are an increasing share of orthodontic patients and often care about both treatment duration and facial and dental aesthetics, which is part of the demand for faster methods.[5][6] Conventional treatment is described as averaging around 20 months, and prolonged appliance wear is associated with risks such as root resorption and enamel demineralization, which accelerated approaches aim to reduce.[1][7]
General orthodontic background, including how tooth movement works and how braces and aligners are used, is covered in encyclopedia articles on orthodontics.[6]

Orthodontic tooth movement depends on bone resorption on the compressed side of the tooth and bone formation on the tension side of the periodontal ligament. On the compression side, mechanical strain triggers inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-1, TNF-alpha and prostaglandin E2, which activate osteoclasts through the RANKL pathway; on the tension side, stretching stimulates osteoblasts to lay down new bone.[1] Accelerated approaches aim to amplify these inflammatory and cellular processes.[1]

The surgical branch rests on the regional acceleratory phenomenon, a temporary increase in bone turnover after injury to bone, described by Harold Frost in 1983.[1] Corticotomy cuts only the outer cortical layer, leaving the marrow intact, and orthodontic forces are applied during the window of heightened remodeling. A review of corticotomy-assisted orthodontics traces the technique's history and reports that it has been used particularly in adult patients.[5]

Cyclic vibration devices apply small oscillating forces, typically through a mouthpiece worn for a set period each day, with the intention of stimulating osteoclast and osteoblast activity.[1] AcceleDent Aura, made by OrthoAccel Technologies, is the best-known example and is described in one trial report as a class II device with US FDA clearance using SoftPulse technology.[3] Trials have used it for about 20 minutes per day with fixed braces and with clear aligners.[8][9]

Photobiomodulation uses low-level laser or LED light, proposed to enhance mitochondrial function and tissue proliferation in the periodontal tissues.[1][10] Electrical stimulation has also been tested as an adjunct; a 2024 systematic review located 13 studies of it in humans and included four in its qualitative analysis, while noting increased risk of selection and performance bias in them.[11]

Micro-osteoperforations, marketed in one form as Propel, make small holes in the alveolar bone to induce local inflammation and the regional acceleratory phenomenon without raising a flap.[1][10] Related minimally invasive procedures include piezocision, which uses a piezoelectric blade to make small cuts in the gum and cortical bone, and discision; a clinical comparison of piezocision and discision has been published.[12] Reviews describe these as part of a shift from traditional flap surgery to less invasive approaches.[7]
Injectable platelet-rich fibrin has also been tested for its effect on canine retraction rate and bone-turnover markers.[13]

Corticotomy-assisted orthodontics uses cuts through the cortical bone to speed movement and has a documented history in the literature.[5] Periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics (PAOO) combines selective corticotomy with particulate bone grafting, intended to increase bone volume and support stability; it requires collaboration between orthodontists and periodontists.[1] A 2024 meta-analysis of periodontally accelerated orthodontic therapy compared periodontal tissue changes with conventional orthodontics, with the stated rationale that PAO increases hard tissue and may reduce relapse.[14]

Vibration devices were among the first accelerators sold to patients directly through orthodontic practices. AcceleDent Aura, made by OrthoAccel, is a mouthpiece worn about 20 minutes a day over braces or aligners, and trials have tested it in teenagers with fixed appliances and in adults with clear aligners.[3][9][15] Propel, in contrast, is a procedure performed by an orthodontist that places micro-osteoperforations in the bone; the two products sit at opposite ends of the invasiveness range.[1][10]

Commentary from academic orthodontists has followed the trial results closely. Kevin O'Brien, an orthodontic researcher, reviewed a 2018 triple-blinded randomized trial of AcceleDent with Invisalign by Katchooi and colleagues in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics: roughly 13 adults per group, with 10 of 13 in the active-device group and 11 of 13 in the sham group able to move to one-week aligner changes, and no significant differences in alignment, pain or compliance.[15] He noted that of four AcceleDent trials he knew of, three had found no effect on tooth movement rate, and he described the absence of evidence as becoming overwhelming, while allowing that one trial reported an effect that he regarded as flawed.[15] One later aligner trial in adults reported fewer days per aligner with the device, as described above.[9]

A systematic review and meta-analysis assessed minimally invasive surgical procedures for accelerating tooth movement and their adverse effects.[2] It included four randomized trials with 61 patients, and the quantitative synthesis found a weighted mean difference of 0.65 mm greater canine retraction over one month with the procedures; the authors concluded that evidence was limited and that more research was needed before routine recommendation.[2]

Systematic reviews have also examined alveolar corticotomies and compared corticotomy-assisted with conventional orthodontic treatment.[16][17] A narrative review of corticotomy-accelerated orthodontics described acceleration of treatment rate as much as three times on average and called it the only evidence-based approach among those reviewed, while noting that long-term periodontal and orthodontic outcomes need further investigation.[18] Surgical approaches have been described as accelerating movement 1.5 to 3 times in some studies but as being supported by limited high-quality research.[1]

Surgical adjuncts carry risks including postoperative pain and swelling.[1] A meta-epidemiological study of 91 randomized trials of surgically assisted acceleration found that 54 of them (59.3 percent) did not adhere to the CONSORT item on reporting harms.[19]

A 2025 systematic review of 23 studies (585 participants) examined root resorption after minimally invasive surgical acceleration. It found micro-osteoperforation and piezocision had no significant effect during leveling, alignment and canine retraction in most analyses, with some movement types showing more or less resorption, and rated evidence quality from very low to moderate. The authors noted that direct resorption can occur when procedures are performed too close to the root.[20]
A study of 116 YouTube videos on accelerated orthodontic treatment evaluated their characteristics, content, popularity and viewer assessments.[21]

Vibration devices. A single-blind randomized trial of 40 adolescents with fixed appliances and maxillary premolar extractions found no clinically or statistically significant difference in the rate of space closure with AcceleDent Aura (difference 0.05 mm per month; P = 0.74).[4] A companion trial of 40 adolescents measuring mandibular alignment found no difference in arch perimeter or incisor irregularity at 5, 8 and 10 weeks.[22] A trial of 20 patients found canine distalization rates of 1.06 mm per month in controls versus 1.24 mm per month (maxillary) in the vibration group, a difference that was not statistically significant.[3] A 32-patient randomized trial over four months likewise found no significant difference in canine retraction or pain levels, and root condition was unchanged.[23] A 24-patient split-mouth trial found that an intermittent force protocol sped canine distalization while added AcceleDent vibration did not change the rate.[8]

In contrast, a 2022 controlled clinical trial of 24 adult aligner patients, allocated by whether they accepted the device, reported that those using AcceleDent with a 7-day aligner change interval completed treatment with fewer days per aligner than a 14-day control regimen and reported less pain.[9]

Surgical and minimally invasive approaches. Randomized trials of surgical acceleration have been pooled in systematic reviews, including the 2016 review of minimally invasive procedures and reviews of corticotomy.[2][16][17] A 2023 Cochrane review on non-surgical adjuncts is summarized in Grokipedia as finding low to very low certainty evidence of clinically significant time savings.[1] A 2024 review of electrical stimulation reported meta-analysis results at three and five months with moderate-strength evidence and high risk of bias in the included studies.[11]

timeline.event: Harold Frost describes the regional acceleratory phenomenon, the basis of surgical acceleration.[1]
Review of corticotomy-assisted orthodontics summarizes its history and clinical applications in adults.[5]
Meta-analysis of minimally invasive surgical acceleration and randomized trials of AcceleDent Aura in adolescents published.[2][10]
Randomized trial of AcceleDent Aura on premolar extraction space closure reports no difference.[4]
Meta-epidemiological study finds harms under-reported in surgical acceleration trials; Cochrane review on non-surgical adjuncts summarized as low-certainty.[1][19]
Systematic review examines root resorption after minimally invasive surgical acceleration.[20]
Harold Frost describes the regional acceleratory phenomenon underlying surgical acceleration.[1]
Randomized sham-controlled trial of AcceleDent with Invisalign reports no difference in aligner completion rates.[15]
Cochrane review of non-surgical adjuncts reports low to very low certainty evidence of time savings (per Grokipedia).[1]
